plan.contextChunk: This figure is a plain vector diagram of four arrows stacked one above another, all drawn at the same shallow upward slope so their lengths can be compared at a glance. Each arrow starts from a small filled black dot. The topmost arrow, in dark navy, is by far the longest and is labeled 3v at its head. Below it an orange arrow labeled v runs in the same up-and-to-the-right direction at about a third that length. Beneath the orange one, a teal arrow labeled 1/2 v is half as long as v and again points the same way. The bottom arrow, drawn in red and labeled -v, has its dot at the right end and its arrowhead at the left, so it runs down and to the left while staying parallel to the others and matching v in length. Because all four share a single line of action, the only difference the eye registers is length, plus the reversal in the last one. The arrangement gives the geometric reading of multiplying a vector by a scalar: a positive factor stretches or shrinks the arrow while preserving its heading, and a negative factor turns it back on itself.

interactionPlan.concept: Multiplying a vector by a scalar scales its length and can reverse its direction, but always keeps it parallel to the original vector.
elements: Base vector v (orange arrow pointing up/right), labeled 'v'
Static vector 3v (dark navy arrow pointing up/right), labeled '3v'
Static vector 1/2v (teal arrow pointing up/right), labeled '1/2v'
Static vector -v (red arrow pointing down/left), labeled '-v'
Dynamic vector kv (purple arrow), labeled 'kv', controlled by the slider
Black dots marking the tail (starting point) of each vector

interactions.label: Vector layout
interactions.teaches: Overlaying vectors visually proves they all share the exact same line of action, making the geometric meaning of a scalar multiple clear.

interactions.label: Scalar multiplier k
interactions.teaches: Multiplying by a scalar > 1 stretches the vector, between 0 and 1 shrinks it, and < 0 reverses its direction.

demo_steps.title: Stacked comparison
demo_steps.narration: By stacking the vectors, we can easily compare their lengths side-by-side. Notice that all vectors are perfectly parallel, sharing the same shallow slope.

demo_steps.title: Overlaid comparison
demo_steps.narration: Switching to an overlaid view places all tails at a single origin dot. Now it is obvious that all these scalar multiples lie along a single infinite line.

demo_steps.title: Positive scalars
demo_steps.narration: Positive values of k stretch or shrink the dynamic purple vector without changing its direction.

demo_steps.title: Negative scalars
demo_steps.narration: When k drops below zero, the vector flips to point in the opposite direction (down and to the left), representing a negative scalar multiple.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Scalar multiplication acts only along the vector's line of action — positive scalars change length, while negative scalars change length and flip the direction 180 degrees.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw the 4 static vectors matching the original figure: 3v (dark navy, top, longest), v (orange), 1/2v (teal), -v (red). They point up and to the right at a shallow angle. For -v, the black tail dot is at its rightmost end and the arrowhead is at the left. Add a 5th dynamic vector kv (purple). In 'Stacked' mode, arrange them vertically with independent black dots at each tail. In 'Overlaid' mode, translate all vectors so their tail dots merge at a single shared origin.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for scalar multiplier k: the learner drags k from negative to positive values, the arrow length scales and flips direction when k crosses 0, and scalar multiplication is seen as stretching, shrinking, or reversing a vector.
- Toggle between stacked comparison and overlay: the learner switches from separate arrows to all arrows sharing the same tail, the endpoints line up by scale factor, and equal direction for positive multiples versus opposite direction for negative multiples becomes easier to read.

evaluation.notes: The geometry and interactivity are excellent for demonstrating scalar multiplication, but a text-rendering bug causes all scalar prefixes to disappear, and the extra interactive vector clutters the default view.

Format the '1/2v' label using a Unicode fraction (like '½') or manually construct a stacked fraction to better match the vertical layout in the source figure.
